title: Testing Whether Safety Refusals Are Overfit to Surface Keyword Patterns

original_idea.problem: Whether safety alignment responds to surface lexical features rather than semantic intent has not been carefully ablated.
original_idea.direction: Create 50 harmful prompt pairs: original with keywords and semantically equivalent paraphrase without keywords. Test both on 3 models. Also test inverse (benign + keywords).
original_idea.why_it_matters: If refusals are largely keyword-driven, the safety system provides false assurance.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: keyword vs semantic gap -> reveals false assurance in current systems. But this is a well-known qualitative observation; quantifying it is valuable but incremental rather than revealing a new mechanism.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very accessible: create prompt pairs, run them through models, measure ASR. No ML training needed. Standard API usage. Beginners can do this.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: ASR comparison table (keyword vs paraphrase) plus FPR on inverse cases. Clear methodology. The prompt curation is the main effort.

novelty.reasoning: The observation that safety refusals overfit to surface lexical features is well-established. 'How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States' (EMNLP 2024 Findings) shows alignment associates early concepts with emotion guesses and refines them into reject tokens — a mechanistic explanation of keyword-level refusal. Cross-lingual jailbreak work (Deng et al. ICLR 2024) demonstrates that translated prompts bypass English keyword-based refusals, directly evidencing keyword overfitting. Multi-turn and paraphrase-based attacks (Foot-In-The-Door, EMNLP 2025) already exploit the semantic-vs-keyword gap. The proposed 50-pair ablation is a cleaner version of what exists but the core finding is well-documented.
